Assume AC. Let $\Gamma$ be a discrete subgroup of $\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb C)$, acting by Möbius transformations on the Riemann sphere. Let $\mu$ be a sphere Beltrami coefficient with $\|\mu\|_\infty\le k<1$, invariant under that action: for each $\gamma\in\Gamma$,
$$\mu(\gamma z)\frac{\overline{\gamma'(z)}}{\gamma'(z)}=\mu(z)$$
almost everywhere in finite charts, equivalently as an equality of sphere coefficient classes. Let $f$ be the unique solution of the Beltrami equation for $\mu$ fixing $0,1,\infty$.

Then every $\rho_\mu(\gamma)=f\gamma f^{-1}$ is Möbius, and $\rho_\mu$ is a faithful homomorphism with discrete image. It preserves the order of every element and therefore preserves torsion-freeness. The map $f$ is an orientation-preserving quasiconformal conjugacy with maximal dilatation at most $(1+k)/(1-k)$. If $\mu=0$, this normalized conjugacy and the induced representation are the identity and the original inclusion. No finiteness or finite-generation hypothesis on $\Gamma$ is needed.

full_proof_step_bindings.exact_quote: By [F1], the required normalized $f$ exists. A Möbius transformation is conformal, so the composition formula [F2] gives $\mu_{f\gamma}(z)=\mu(\gamma z)\overline{\gamma'(z)}/\gamma'(z)=\mu(z)$ almost everywhere by the assumed invariance. These are coefficient classes on the sphere; poles are handled in its other chart and the finitely many omitted points are null. Thus $f\gamma$ and $f$ solve the same sphere Beltrami equation. Uniqueness up to Möbius postcomposition in [F1] gives a Möbius map $A_\gamma$ with $f\gamma=A_\gamma f$, proving $A_\gamma=f\gamma f^{-1}$. [A1, F1, F2, given]

Conjugation by the bijection $f$ preserves products and is injective, so $\gamma\mapsto A_\gamma$ is a faithful homomorphism. Its restriction to every cyclic subgroup is an isomorphism, preserving element orders, including infinite order. Its image therefore is torsion-free exactly when the original group is. [step 1.1, algebra]

We check discreteness in the actual matrix topology. Suppose otherwise. The finite-dimensional matrix group is metrizable, so there would be nonidentity elements $A_{\gamma_n}$ tending to the identity. Their sphere actions converge uniformly to the identity: in homogeneous coordinates unit vectors map to their matrix images, and matrices tending to a scalar identity give uniformly convergent projective actions on the compact unit sphere. Uniform continuity of $f^{-1}$ on the compact sphere then gives $\gamma_n=f^{-1}A_{\gamma_n}f\to\mathrm{id}$ uniformly on the sphere. For completeness, uniform convergence of Möbius maps to the identity implies convergence in the matrix group. Their values on $0,1,\infty$ converge to these three distinct points. The unique fractional linear map with three specified distinct images is obtained by composing the maps $z\mapsto((z-a)/(z-c))((b-c)/(b-a))$ taking an ordered triple $(a,b,c)$ to $(0,1,\infty)$, interpreted in the appropriate finite charts. Its projective matrix coefficients depend continuously on the three images near $(0,1,\infty)$. Thus $\gamma_n\to\mathrm{id}$ in $\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb C)$, contrary to discreteness of $\Gamma$. Hence the image is discrete. [step 1.1, given, algebra]

The dilatation and orientation claims are exactly those of [F1]. If $\mu=0$, the identity sphere map solves the equation and has the chosen normalization, so [F1]'s uniqueness gives $f=\mathrm{id}$ and $\rho_\mu(\gamma)=\gamma$. The trivial group and finite groups are included; no selected generating set or countable family of exceptional sets was used, since step 1.1 proves the coefficient identity separately for each supplied group element. [F1, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 2.2] ∎

Assume AC. Let $X$ be a connected Riemann surface obtained from a compact Riemann surface by removing finitely many points, and let $p:Y\to X$ be a connected unbranched holomorphic covering. Let $Q(X)$ and $Q(Y)$ be their spaces of integrable holomorphic quadratic differentials, with norm $\|q\|_1=\int|q|$. Suppose a finite set of based loops generates $\pi_1(X)$ and its monodromy graph on a fiber of $p$ has positive vertex expansion: there is $\gamma>0$ such that
$$|b(V)|\ge\gamma|V|$$
for every finite set of vertices $V$, where $b(V)$ consists of vertices outside $V$ adjacent to $V$. This is the nonamenability hypothesis, stated for the actual covering rather than only for a deck group.

The pushforward
$$\Theta_p:Q(Y)\longrightarrow Q(X),\qquad \Theta_pq=\sum_{\text{local inverse branches }s}s^*q$$
is well defined and has operator norm strictly less than one. Thus there is $c=c(X,p)<1$ with $\|\Theta_pq\|_1\le c\|q\|_1$ for every $q$. No finite generation of $\pi_1(Y)$, regularity of the covering, or compactness of $Y$ is assumed. No bound uniform over varying complex structures on $X$ is asserted here.

full_proof_step_bindings.exact_quote: The covering fiber is countable: it is a transitive monodromy set for the finitely generated, hence countable, fundamental group. On a relatively compact coordinate disk $D$ in $X$, the pullbacks of an integrable $q$ from its inverse sheets have total absolute integral at most $\|q\|_1$. By the local mean-value bound [F1], on any smaller disk their absolute values have summable uniform bounds. Their sum therefore converges normally and is holomorphic. Changing coordinates or sheet order gives the same sum, so it defines $\Theta_pq$. Integration of the pointwise triangle inequality over coordinate pieces, followed by summing the sheet integrals, gives $\|\Theta_pq\|_1\le\|q\|_1$. [A1, F1, given, construct, algebra]

We need a local qualitative rigidity fact. If holomorphic $h$ on the unit disk satisfies $\int|h|=1$ and $\operatorname{Re}\int h\ge1-\epsilon$, then $\|h-1/\pi\|_1\to0$ uniformly as $\epsilon\to0$. Indeed $|\operatorname{Im}h|^2\le2|h|(|h|-\operatorname{Re}h)$ gives $\int|\operatorname{Im}h|\le\sqrt{2\epsilon}$. By [F1], these functions are locally bounded and $\operatorname{Re}h(0)=\pi^{-1}\operatorname{Re}\int h\to1/\pi$. Every subsequential limit supplied by [F3] is therefore the real constant $1/\pi$. Thus the whole family converges locally uniformly to that constant. On a concentric radius-$r$ disk the absolute integral tends to $r^2$, so the integral outside it tends to $1-r^2$. Splitting the $L^1$ difference into these two pieces and then taking $r\uparrow1$ proves the claim. If uniformity failed, a sequence with $\epsilon\to0$ and distance bounded below would contradict this argument. Translation, dilation and multiplication by a constant phase give the same conclusion on any Euclidean disk, with normalized constant density. [F1, F3, algebra]

The closed unit ball of $Q(X)$ is compact in its $L^1$ norm. First, at a removed point choose a puncture coordinate $z$. If $q=f(z)dz^2$ is integrable, put $M(r)=(2\pi)^{-1}\int_0^{2\pi}|f(re^{it})|dt$. Since $\int_0^{r_0}rM(r)dr<\infty$, some $r_j\downarrow0$ satisfy $r_j^2M(r_j)\to0$. The Laurent coefficient formula [F2] gives $|a_{-m}|\le r_j^mM(r_j)\to0$ for $m\ge2$. Thus $f=a_{-1}/z+h(z)$ with $h$ holomorphic across the puncture. For a unit-norm family, [F1] uniformly bounds $f$ on one fixed circle surrounding that puncture, since this circle has a compact neighborhood inside $X$. Its contour integral uniformly bounds $a_{-1}$; Cauchy's formula then bounds $h$ on the smaller disk. Consequently $\int_{|z|<r}|f(z)|\,dxdy\le C(r+r^2)$ uniformly. Away from the finitely many punctures, [F1] and [F3], applied in finitely many coordinate charts and then diagonally on an exhaustion, give locally uniformly convergent subsequences of any unit-ball sequence. Their limits agree under quadratic-differential coordinate changes. The uniform puncture-tail bound upgrades convergence to $L^1$ on all of $X$, with limiting norm at most one. This proves the asserted compactness. [A1, F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

Suppose for contradiction that $\|\Theta_p\|=1$. Choose $q_n\in Q(Y)$ of norm one with $\|\Theta_pq_n\|_1\to1$. By step 2.1, after a subsequence $\Theta_pq_n\to\psi$ in $L^1$, where $\|\psi\|_1=1$. Set $\mu=\overline\psi/|\psi|$ away from its zeros and zero at its zeros; this is a Beltrami differential, so $q\mu$ is an integrable density. Then $$I_n=\int_Y\bigl(|q_n|-\operatorname{Re}(q_np^*\mu)\bigr)=1-\operatorname{Re}\int_X(\Theta_pq_n)\mu\longrightarrow0.$$ The integrand is everywhere nonnegative. The zeros of $\psi$ are discrete and its puncture extensions are meromorphic by step 2.1. Choose representatives of the finite generating loops avoiding those zeros. On their compact union the flat metric $|\psi|$ has a positive local coordinate radius: locally $\psi=dw^2$, by taking a local square root of its nonvanishing holomorphic coefficient and integrating it. Cover the generating loops by finitely many sufficiently small equal-radius flat disks $E_1,\ldots,E_J$, with connected union $U$, connected pairwise intersections whenever nonempty, and a common flat area $A>0$. The disks can be chosen with each radius less than one quarter of the minimum flat coordinate radius on a compact neighborhood of the loops. Intersecting disks then lie in one larger flat chart, so their intersection is the usual connected Euclidean lens. Their union carries every generating loop. [A1, step 2.1, step 1.2, construct, algebra]

Let $\mathcal G$ be the intersection graph of all lifted disks. It is connected because $U$ carries $\pi_1(X)$ and $Y$ is connected. Every vertex has degree at most $J-1$: a lift of one disk meets at most one lift of any other, because their base intersection is connected. Its vertex expansion is some $\gamma_0>0$. Here are the comparison details. Choose one disk as anchor. Paths through the finite base disk graph give a constant $C$ such that every lifted vertex is within $C$ graph edges of an anchor vertex. Each supplied generator loop gives a disk chain of length at most one common $L$ joining the anchor vertices related by that generator's monodromy. For a finite lifted vertex set $S$, let $T$ be the anchor vertices within distance $C$ of $S$. If $D=\max(2,J)$, then $|T|\ge |S|/D^{C+1}$. At least $\gamma|T|$ anchor vertices lie in its monodromy border. Each lies within $L+C$ edges of $b(S)$: join its neighboring anchor to $S$ by a path of length at most $C$, then follow the generator chain; its endpoint is outside $T$, so the combined path must exit $S$. Bounded degree implies $\gamma|T|\le D^{L+C+2}|b(S)|$. This gives a fixed positive $\gamma_0$, for example $\gamma D^{-(L+2C+3)}$. [given, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

For a lifted disk $B$ define its mass $m_n(B)=\int_B|q_n|$ and inefficiency $i_n(B)=m_n(B)^{-1}\int_B(|q_n|-\operatorname{Re}(q_np^*\mu))$. A zero-mass disk would make $q_n$ identically zero on connected $Y$, so no such disk occurs. Let $a>0$ be the minimum, over the finitely many nonempty base lenses, of their flat area divided by $A$. On each lifted disk, step 1.2 says that if $i_n(B)<\epsilon$, then $q_n$ is within $\eta m_n(B)$ in $L^1$ of $(m_n(B)/A)p^*\psi$, where $\eta\to0$ uniformly with $\epsilon$. Thus neighboring efficient disks have mass ratio at least $(a-\eta)/(a+\eta)$ in either direction, by integrating their two errors on the common lens. If only $B$ is efficient, its neighbor $B'$ still has mass at least $(a-\eta)m_n(B)$, because it contains that lens. Choose $\eta<a/2$ small enough that $\lambda=(a-\eta)/(a+\eta)$ satisfies $\lambda^{-1}-1<\gamma_0/2$, and choose a fixed $\epsilon>0$ that ensures this error bound. These choices are independent of $n$. [step 1.2, step 3.1, step 4.1, algebra]

We spell out the weighted expansion estimate used on this graph. For a vertex subset $V$ and an integrable positive function $m$ on it with neighboring ratios at least $\lambda$, put $F(w)=\sup\{m(v):v\in V,\ v\sim w\}$ for $w\notin V$. Layer-cake integration of $|b(\{v\in V:m(v)>t\})|\ge\gamma_0|\{v\in V:m(v)>t\}|$ gives $$\sum_{w\notin V}F(w)\ge\bigl(\gamma_0-(\lambda^{-1}-1)\bigr)\sum_{v\in V}m(v).$$ Indeed an outside vertex contributes at most $F(w)$ to the integrated border. An inside vertex with value $m(v)$ can belong to that border only for $m(v)\le t<\lambda^{-1}m(v)$, so its contribution is at most $(\lambda^{-1}-1)m(v)$. Each positive superlevel set is finite because $m$ is summable; integrating the counting inequalities and interchanging nonnegative sums proves the formula, also for infinite $V$. [step 4.1, step 5.1, algebra]

Apply step 6.1 to the efficient vertices $V_n=\{B:i_n(B)<\epsilon\}$ and $m=m_n$. Summability holds because a point lies in at most $J$ lifted disks and $\|q_n\|_1=1$. Every vertex in $b(V_n)$ is inefficient and, by step 5.1, has mass at least $(a-\eta)F(w)$. Hence, writing $W_n$ for all inefficient vertices, $$\sum_{B\in W_n}m_n(B)\ge (a-\eta)\gamma_0\sum_{B\in V_n}m_n(B)/2.$$ On the other hand, since the nonnegative inefficiency integrand is counted at most $J$ times, $$J I_n\ge\sum_{B\in W_n}m_n(B)i_n(B)\ge\epsilon\sum_{B\in W_n}m_n(B).$$ As $I_n\to0$, both the inefficient and, by the first inequality, efficient mass sums tend to zero. But their total is at least $\int_{p^{-1}U}|q_n|\ge\int_U|\Theta_pq_n|$, which tends to $\int_U|\psi|>0$. This contradiction proves $\|\Theta_p\|<1$. If $Q(X)=0$, the operator is zero and the assertion holds immediately; otherwise the preceding contradiction covers every possibility. All constants may depend on $X$, its generating net and the actual covering, as allowed. [step 1.1, step 3.1, step 5.1, step 6.1, algebra] ∎

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\Gamma\le\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb R)$ be a supplied discrete torsion-free finite-coarea Fuchsian group. Write $H^+=\{\operatorname{Im}z>0\}$, $H^-=\{\operatorname{Im}z<0\}$ and $R=\mathbb R\cup\{\infty\}$. The reference Riemann surfaces and their holomorphic universal coverings are $X^\pm=H^\pm/\Gamma$ and $\pi^\pm:H^\pm\to X^\pm$. Supply their finite-type puncture compactifications and matching cusp labels. More explicitly, each puncture label $j$ specifies a conjugacy class of maximal parabolic subgroups $P_j=\langle\gamma_j\rangle$, its fixed point $\xi_j\in R$ up to $\Gamma$, and its puncture on each $X^\pm$; these are all the parabolic classes. Choose $\gamma_j$ positively around the upper puncture. The positive lower puncture loop then represents $\gamma_j^{-1}$. This cusp identification is part of the supplied marked reference model.

Let $Y^\pm$ be compact Riemann surfaces with finitely many labeled points removed, and let $m^\pm:X^\pm\to Y^\pm$ be supplied orientation-preserving quasiconformal homeomorphisms of finite maximal dilatations $K_\pm$. Require their extensions to the puncture compactifications to send every label to its corresponding label. The lower marking preserves the complex orientation of $H^-$; under reflection $H^+\to H^-$ it is the oppositely oriented surface marking.

There exist a normalized orientation-preserving quasiconformal sphere homeomorphism $f$ and a discrete faithful representation $\rho:\Gamma\to\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb C)$ such that $\rho(\gamma)=f\gamma f^{-1}$ and $K_f\le\max\{K_+,K_-\}$. The limit set of $G=\rho(\Gamma)$ is the quasicircle $C=f(R)$, and its full domain of discontinuity is the union of the two invariant simply connected domains $\Omega^\pm=f(H^\pm)$. Thus $G$ is quasifuchsian in this explicit sense, as well as being a quasiconformal deformation of the supplied cofinite Fuchsian group.

The induced quotient homeomorphisms $\overline f^\pm:X^\pm\to\Omega^\pm/G$ satisfy
$$I^\pm:=m^\pm\circ(\overline f^\pm)^{-1}:\Omega^\pm/G\longrightarrow Y^\pm,$$
where both $I^\pm$ are biholomorphic. In particular the two prescribed marked conformal boundary structures are realized simultaneously, with the exact markings $I^\pm\overline f^\pm=m^\pm$.

Parabolic elements are preserved in both directions. Each labeled maximal subgroup $P_j$ becomes the maximal parabolic subgroup $\rho(P_j)$ fixing $f(\xi_j)$, and its primitive marked generator is exactly $\rho(\gamma_j)$; the positive lower puncture generator remains its inverse. Under $I^\pm$ the puncture labels agree with the supplied labels on $Y^\pm$. No assertion of uniqueness on Teichmüller classes, holomorphic dependence, a skinning-map fixed point, or hyperbolization is included.

Countable chart subcovers of the half-planes assemble the measurable fields and their exceptional null sets. For each $\gamma\in\Gamma$, $\pi^\pm\gamma=\pi^\pm$ gives $(\widetilde

We give the group-action details that identify the full domain of discontinuity. A discrete subgroup of the finite-dimensional matrix group is closed: if distinct elements converged to any matrix-group point, quotients of consecutive convergent elements would be nonidentity elements tending to the identity, contradicting discreteness. Its intersection with a compact set is finite by the same subsequence argument. On the upper half-plane, a matrix sending $i$ to $x+iy$ is $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}\sqrt y&x/\sqrt y\\0&1/\sqrt y\end{smallmatrix}\right)$, up to the compact stabilizer $\mathrm{PSO}(2)$ of $i$. This exhibits the properness of the model action over compact subsets and shows that the orbit $\Gamma i$ has no accumulation in $H^+$. Its boundary accumulation set $\Lambda\subseteq R$ in the closed-disc compactification is closed and $\Gamma$-invariant. For any sequence of distinct elements, choose determinant-one real lifts $A_n$. Their matrix norms tend to infinity after passing to a subsequence, since a norm bound gives a compact set of determinant-one matrices. Normalize and pass to $A_n/\|A_n\|\to A\ne0$; its determinant is zero, so it has rank one. On the sphere the corresponding Möbius maps tend locally uniformly to the image line $a$ off the kernel line $b$. Both lines are real. Evaluating at $i$ gives $a\in\Lambda$, and applying the same calculation to inverses gives $b\in\Lambda$; for a two-by-two rank-one limit the inverse's image is the original kernel. Conversely every point of $\Lambda$ is an attracting line of such a subsequence. These elementary matrix limits fix the limit-set convention being used. [A1, given, construct, algebra]

Define a finite-chart coefficient $\mu$ by $\mu=\widetilde\nu^+$ on $H^+$, $\mu=\widetilde\nu^-$ on $H^-$ and $\mu=0$ on the real axis. The axis is area-null. Use the inversion pullback law in [F1] to define its infinity-chart class; the value at infinity is immaterial. Thus it is a sphere coefficient with $\|\mu\|_\infty\le k$. Every $\gamma\in\Gamma$ preserves both half-planes and their common real circle, so step 1.1 proves the required sphere invariance. Apply [F2] to obtain $f$ fixing $0,1,\infty$ and the faithful discrete representation $\rho(\gamma)=f\gamma f^{-1}$. Its image is torsion-free because element orders are preserved. The bound in [F2] gives $K_f\le(1+k)/(1-k)=\max\{K_+,K_-\}$. [A1, F1, F2, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

Finite coarea forces $\Lambda=R$. First, if $\Lambda$ is empty, the proper orbit in step 1.2 is finite, because an infinite subset of the compact closed disc has an accumulation point. Its stabilizer lies in the compact rotation group and is finite by discreteness; torsion-freeness makes that stabilizer trivial. Thus $\Gamma$ is finite and hence trivial, whose hyperbolic-plane quotient has infinite area. If $\Lambda$ is one point, conjugate it to infinity. All group elements then have the form $z\mapsto az+b$ with $a>0$, $b$ real. If an element has $a\ne1$, it has a second, finite fixed point $c$. Any element not fixing $c$ has a nonidentity translation as its commutator with this element, since affine multipliers commute and affine maps with the same finite fixed point commute. Conjugating that translation by powers of the dilation shrinks it to the identity, impossible for a discrete group. Hence all elements would fix $c$; powers of the dilation then make $c$ a second orbit accumulation point, another contradiction. Therefore all elements are translations. Their discrete translation lengths form a cyclic additive subgroup of $\mathbb R$ (or zero); the quotient has infinite area, since the area integral on a fixed-width vertical strip is $\int_0^1y^{-2}dy=\infty$. These cases are excluded. Now suppose $\Lambda$ is a proper subset with at least two points. Choose a component interval $J$ of $R\setminus\Lambda$, and let $V_J$ be the open hyperbolic half-plane bounded by the geodesic joining its endpoints and facing $J$. Distinct translates of $J$ are distinct complementary intervals, so the corresponding open half-planes are disjoint. Consequently $V_J/\Gamma_J$ embeds in $H^+/\Gamma$, where $\Gamma_J$ stabilizes $J$. A real orientation-preserving Möbius map stabilizing this interval fixes its endpoints individually. Conjugate them to $0,\infty$, with $J$ the positive real interval. Then $V_J=\{\operatorname{Re}z>0,\operatorname{Im}z>0\}$ and $\Gamma_J$ consists of positive dilations. Discreteness makes it cyclic or trivial. In coordinates $z=r e^{i\theta}$ the area is $(dr/r)d\theta/\sin^2\theta$. A radial interval $1\le r\le a$ is a fundamental interval for a nontrivial dilation $r\mapsto ar$, and its area for $0<\theta<\pi/2$ is infinite; in the trivial case the subregion $1\le r\le2$ already has infinite area. This embedded infinite-area region contradicts finite coarea. All proper $\Lambda$ are excluded. [step 1.2, given, cases, construct, algebra]

Put $\Omega^\pm=f(H^\pm)$ and $C=f(R)$. These are two simply connected domains separated by the Jordan curve $C$, because $f$ is a sphere homeomorphism; $C$ is a quasicircle by its displayed quasiconformal parametrization. Conjugacy makes both domains invariant. The original deck actions on $H^\pm$ are free and properly discontinuous, and their conjugates have the same properties on $\Omega^\pm$. The quotient maps $q^\pm:\Omega^\pm\to\Omega^\pm/G$ are therefore unbranched coverings. Their Riemann surface charts are the charts of any sufficiently small injective sheet, with transition maps in $G$, hence holomorphic. The maps $f|_{H^\pm}$ descend to homeomorphisms $\overline f^\pm:X^\pm\to\Omega^\pm/G$ satisfying $q^\pm f=\overline f^\pm\pi^\pm$. No extension across the real circle is used in constructing these quotient complex structures. [step 2.1, given, construct, algebra]

The map $I^\pm=m^\pm(\overline f^\pm)^{-1}$ is a homeomorphism. On a small sheet its lift to $\Omega^\pm$ is $m^\pm\pi^\pm f^{-1}$. Restrict $\pi^\pm$ to an injective sheet and choose a target chart for $m^\pm$ there. The two local quasiconformal homeomorphisms $m^\pm\pi^\pm$ and $f$ on this source sheet have the same coefficient, namely $\widetilde\nu^\pm$, by steps 1.1 and 2.1. Their composition with $f^{-1}$ is therefore $1$-quasiconformal by [F3]. The same supplier makes it biholomorphic in these charts, including its inverse. As this is true around every point, $I^\pm$ are biholomorphic globally. Their definition gives the exact marked identities in the Statement. This argument uses local equal-coefficient cancellation, not a claimed global uniqueness theorem for maps on punctured surfaces. [F3, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra]

The boundary convergence limit set of $G$ is exactly $f(\Lambda)=C$. Indeed a rank-one subsequential convergence $\gamma_n\to a$ off $b$ from step 1.2 becomes $f\gamma_nf^{-1}\to f(a)$ locally uniformly off $f(b)$, by uniform continuity of sphere homeomorphisms on compact sets. Conversely, for any sequence of distinct elements in $G$, apply step 1.2 to its preimages and pass to that subsequence. Since the conjugates are Möbius, their own normalized complex matrix limits have rank one; testing at a point different from the two exceptional kernel points identifies their attracting line with $f(a)$. Thus there are no other attracting limits, and each point of $C$ occurs, by step 2.2. This is also the usual hyperbolic-orbit limit set: if $B_n/\|B_n\|\to B$ has rank one and $P$ is a positive Hermitian determinant-one matrix representing a point of $\mathbb H^3$, then the projective limit of $B_nPB_n^*$ is the nonzero rank-one matrix $BPB^*$, whose image is the attracting line. This calculation is the positive-Hermitian model of the Möbius action and shows equivalence of the two definitions here. Off $C$, the action is properly discontinuous by step 3.1. Every open neighborhood $U$ of $x$ contains a point $z\ne y$; eventually the images of $z$ lie in $U$, so infinitely many group elements have $gU\cap U\ne\varnothing$. Thus no point of $C$ belongs to the domain of discontinuity. The full domain is exactly $\Omega^+\sqcup\Omega^-$, as claimed. [step 2.1, step 3.1, step 1.2, step 2.2, algebra]

Assume AC. Fix a disk $D_R\subset\mathbb C$ and let $B_R$ be the complex Banach space of essentially bounded measurable coefficients supported in $D_R$. For every $\mu\in B_R$ with $\|\mu\|_\infty<1$, there is exactly one quasiconformal sphere homeomorphism $f^\mu$ with coefficient $\mu$ and principal normalization
$$f^\mu(z)=z+O(1/z)\quad(z\to\infty).$$
For every $0\le\kappa<1$ there is $p>2$ such that, on $\|\mu\|_\infty<\kappa$, writing $\mathcal B$ and $\mathcal C$ for the Beurling and Cauchy transforms,
$$h_\mu=(I-\mu\mathcal B)^{-1}\mu,\qquad f^\mu=z+\mathcal Ch_\mu.$$
Here $h_\mu$ is supported in $D_R$, the map $\mu\mapsto h_\mu$ is holomorphic into $L^p(\mathbb C)$, and $\mu\mapsto f^\mu-z$ is holomorphic into $W^{1,p}(\mathbb C)$ and into bounded Hölder functions of exponent $1-2/p$. In particular $f^\mu(z)$ depends holomorphically on $\mu$ for every fixed finite $z$.

On $\mathbb C\setminus\overline D_R$, the Schwarzian
$$S(f^\mu)=\frac{(f^\mu)'''}{(f^\mu)'}-\frac32\left(\frac{(f^\mu)''}{(f^\mu)'}\right)^2$$
is holomorphic jointly in the coefficient parameter and in the spatial variable, in the sense of holomorphic dependence into the compact-open space of holomorphic functions. Its derivative at zero is
$$D S(f^0)[\nu](z)=-\frac6\pi\int_{D_R}\frac{\nu(w)}{(z-w)^4}\,dA(w).$$
The result asserts local coefficient dependence; it does not identify a marked surface deformation quotient or prove its dimension.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\Sigma$ be a compact connected Riemann surface of genus $g$, let $P=\{p_1,\ldots,p_n\}$ be a finite labeled set, possibly empty, and suppose $2g-2+n>0$. Put $X=\Sigma\setminus P$, let $K$ be the canonical bundle and $T=K^*$ the holomorphic tangent line bundle, and set $E=T\otimes\mathcal O(-P)$. Its holomorphic sections are holomorphic vector fields vanishing at every marked point. In a coordinate centered at $p_j$, the inclusion $E\to T$ sends a local frame of $E$ to $z\partial_z$.

Let $B^\infty(X)$ be the complex vector space of measurable Beltrami tensors, written $\mu(z)d\bar z\otimes\partial_z$, with $\|\mu\|_\infty<\infty$. Here there is no strict bound below one: this is the full linear space of bounded infinitesimal coefficients. The coordinate rule for its scalar coefficient is the usual modulus-one Beltrami rule. Finite point sets do not affect its almost-everywhere classes, so these tensors are also locally bounded $T$-valued $(0,1)$-forms on $\Sigma$.

Define $\mathcal V_P$ to consist of continuous sections $v$ of $T$ on all of $\Sigma$, vanishing at every $p_j$, for which the distributional derivative $\bar\partial_Tv$ belongs to $B^\infty(X)$. This derivative is taken in holomorphic frames on $\Sigma$, including at marked points. Define the analytic marked infinitesimally trivial coefficients and their quotient by
$$N_P=\bar\partial_T\mathcal V_P,\qquad \mathcal T_P=B^\infty(X)/N_P,\qquad \|[\mu]\|=\inf_{\nu\in N_P}\|\mu-\nu\|_\infty.$$
Let $Q(X)=H^0(\Sigma,K^2\otimes\mathcal O(P))$. Thus its elements are holomorphic quadratic differentials on $X$ with at most simple poles at the marked points. Give it the norm $\|q\|_1=\int_X|\phi(z)|\,dx\,dy$ for $q=\phi(z)dz^2$.

Then:

1. Every $v\in\mathcal V_P$ is locally log-Lipschitz: in a fixed coordinate disc, $|v(z+h)-v(z)|\le C|h|(1+|\log|h||)$ on smaller compact discs. In particular, $v(z)=O(|z|(1+|\log|z||))$ at a marked point where its value is zero. No Sobolev differentiability stronger than the stated distributional condition is assumed.
2. For $\mu\in B^\infty(X)$, there is $v\in\mathcal V_P$ with $\bar\partial_Tv=\mu$ if and only if
$$\langle\mu,q\rangle:=\int_X\mu(z)\phi(z)\,dx\,dy=0\quad\text{for every }q\in Q(X).$$
When it exists, this marked primitive is unique. Consequently $N_P$ is closed in the essential-supremum norm.
3. There is a canonical complex-linear isomorphism $\mathcal T_P\cong H^1(\Sigma,E)$. Both this space and $Q(X)$ have dimension $3g-3+n$. The pairing above induces an isometric complex-linear identification
$$Q(X)\xrightarrow{\sim}(\mathcal T_P)^*,$$
and the quotient norm is exactly
$$\|[\mu]\|=\sup_{q\in Q(X),\ \|q\|_1\le1}|\langle\mu,q\rangle|.$$
The holomorphic quadratic differentials on $X$ integrable in this coordinate-invariant $L^1$ norm are exactly $Q(X)$.

This is the analytic marked Beltrami deformation quotient, including its cohomological and norm-dual identifications. It does not assert that a global Teichmüller manifold has been constructed or identify a derivative of a global moduli projection without such a separate construction.

full_proof_step_bindings.exact_quote: The norms and bilinear pairing in the Statement are intrinsic. Under a holomorphic coordinate change $z=\psi(\zeta)$ one has $\mu_\zeta=(\mu_z\circ\psi)\overline{\psi'}/\psi'$ and $\phi_\zeta=(\phi_z\circ\psi)(\psi')^2$. Thus $|\mu_\zeta|=|\mu_z\circ\psi|$, $|\phi_\zeta|\,dA_\zeta=|\phi_z|\,dA_z$ and $\mu_\zeta\phi_\zeta\,dA_\zeta=\mu_z\phi_z\,dA_z$. Holomorphic coordinate changes and their inverses preserve null sets locally, so these are equalities of the stated measurable classes. A simple pole has coefficient $O(1/|z|)$, integrable against $dA$, proving $Q(X)\subset L^1$. Conversely, if a quadratic coefficient $\phi$ is holomorphic and integrable on a punctured disc, write $A(r)=\int_0^{2\pi}|\phi(re^{it})|\,dt$. Integrability is $\int_0^\epsilon rA(r)dr<\infty$, so there are radii $r_k\to0$ with $r_k^2A(r_k)\to0$; otherwise the integral would dominate a positive multiple of $\int_0^\epsilon dr/r$. For each $j\ge2$, the Laurent coefficient formula in [F4] gives $|a_{-j}|\le r_k^jA(r_k)/(2\pi)\to0$. All coefficients of pole order at least two vanish, including every such coefficient of a potential essential singularity. The Laurent expansion therefore has at most a simple pole. This proves the asserted exact integrable class. [A1, F4, given, algebra]

We supply the needed bounded-data local primitive. Let $b$ be bounded and supported in a fixed planar disc, and put $Cb(z)=\pi^{-1}\int b(\zeta)/(z-\zeta)\,dA_\zeta$. The kernel $1/z$ is locally integrable, so this integral exists and is bounded on compact sets by $C\|b\|_\infty$. The distribution identity $\bar\partial(1/(\pi z))=\delta_0$ follows directly by integrating a compactly supported smooth test function on the complement of a radius-$r$ disc: Stokes gives $-\pi^{-1}\int (\bar\partial\eta)/z\,dA\to\eta(0)$, since the inner boundary integral of $\eta(z)/z$ tends to $-2\pi i\eta(0)$. Fubini applies to the locally integrable kernel against a compactly supported test derivative and the bounded compactly supported $b$, and gives $\bar\partial Cb=b$ distributionally. To bound differences at points a distance $h$ apart, set $r=|h|$. On the union of radius-$2r$ discs about those points, the separate kernel integrals are $O(r\|b\|_\infty)$. Outside that union, the kernel difference is at most $Cr/|z-\zeta|^2$. Integration in polar coordinates from radius $2r$ to a fixed larger radius gives $Cr(1+|\log r|)\|b\|_\infty$. Hence $Cb$ is continuous and log-Lipschitz on fixed compact sets. All constants may depend on the fixed discs. This proves the local analytic estimate, without a Calderón–Zygmund or global $L^p$ solvability assertion. [given, construct, algebra]

A continuous function $a$ whose distributional $\bar\partial a$ is bounded is locally the sum of a log-Lipschitz function and a holomorphic function. Indeed, multiply its bounded derivative by a smooth cutoff equal to one on a smaller disc, apply step 1.2, and subtract that Cauchy primitive. The difference has distributional $\bar\partial$ zero. Distributional derivatives commute, so its Laplacian $4\partial\bar\partial$ is zero. By [F4] it is smooth; its Cauchy–Riemann equation makes it holomorphic. Equality of the smooth representative and the continuous difference is pointwise, since two continuous functions equal almost everywhere agree everywhere. A holomorphic function has bounded derivative on a smaller compact disc, so is Lipschitz there. This proves the log-Lipschitz assertion. The same argument applies in a holomorphic vector-bundle frame, proving the first assertion for every $v\in\mathcal V_P$. If $v(p)=0$, subtracting its value gives $|v(z)|\le C|z|(1+|\log|z||)$ in a coordinate centered at $p$. [A1, F4, step 1.2, algebra]

For an arbitrary bounded $\mu$ we now reduce to smooth compact Dolbeault data. Choose finitely many holomorphic coordinate/frame discs $U_i$ with larger coordinate discs $V_i$ containing their closures. Near each marked point, arrange that a single one of these discs contains it and all other discs avoid a smaller fixed neighborhood of that point. This is done by taking disjoint marked coordinate discs first and then covering the compact complement of smaller marked discs. Use [F4] to choose a subordinate smooth partition $\chi_i$; the designated marked-disc function equals one near its marked point. On $V_i$ multiply the local coefficient of $\mu$ by a cutoff equal to one near $\overline U_i$, extend by zero, and use step 1.2 to construct a local continuous log-Lipschitz vector field $v_i$ with $\bar\partial_Tv_i=\mu$ on $U_i$. For a marked disc subtract its value at the marked point, a constant multiple of its holomorphic coordinate frame, so that $v_i(p_j)=0$. The field $v_0$ is continuous, vanishes at all marked points and is locally log-Lipschitz. [A1, F4, step 1.2, construct, algebra]

Every $\bar\partial_Tv$ with $v\in\mathcal V_P$ annihilates $Q(X)$. Write $q=\phi dz^2$ and contract it with $v$ to get the globally defined $(1,0)$-form $\alpha=v\phi dz$ on $X$. In each transition annulus, step 2.1 gives $|v|\le Cr(1+|\log r|)$ and the simple-pole bound gives $|\phi|\le C/r$. Its area is $O(r^2)$, so this last integral is $O(r(1+|\log r|))$, tending to zero. Dominated convergence on the left is valid because the coefficient is bounded and $q$ is integrable by step 1.1. If $P$ is empty take $\eta_r=1$ and the same identity has right side zero. Thus $N_P\subseteq Q(X)^\perp$. This argument requires the continuous marked value and its proved regularity, rather than a point value assigned to a mere $L^p$ representative. [step 1.1, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

The residual $\beta$ is actually smooth, despite the merely bounded original data. On a neighborhood inside $U_j$, subtract $v_j$ from every summand using $\sum_i\bar\partial\chi_i=0$: $\beta=-\sum_i(\bar\partial\chi_i)(v_i-v_j)$. On each overlap $v_i-v_j$ has distributional $\bar\partial_T$ zero and is holomorphic by the argument of step 2.1. The products therefore are smooth, including their zero extensions away from compact partition supports. Near a marked point the single partition function is one and all derivatives of partition functions vanish, so $\beta=0$ there. Consequently $\beta$ is a smooth $E$-valued $(0,1)$-form, using $E=T(-P)$ away from the marked points and its zero extension near them. Also $\bar\partial_Tv_0=\mu-\beta$ is bounded, hence $v_0\in\mathcal V_P$. Step 3.1 yields $\langle\mu,q\rangle=\langle\beta,q\rangle$ for all $q\in Q(X)$. This is the promised full marked bounded-data reduction; dividing a bounded coefficient by $z$ and then assuming an unproved $L^p$ theorem is unnecessary. [step 2.1, step 3.1, step 2.2, algebra]

Apply compact Dolbeault and Serre duality precisely to $E$. By [F3] choose a nonzero meromorphic differential and its canonical divisor $K_0$. Then [F1] identifies $E\cong\mathcal O(-K_0-P)$ and $K\otimes E^*\cong K^2(P)$, so [F2] applies to exactly this bundle and its quadratic dual. Choose auxiliary compatible metrics using [F1]; their choice changes none of the cohomology or pairings. The construction $\mu\mapsto[\beta]$ is canonical. Fixing one of the finite covers, cutoffs and Cauchy formulas in step 2.2 makes it complex linear, since subtraction of the local value at a marked point also is linear. With any other choices, the two resulting residuals have the same pairings against every $q$ by step 4.1. The perfect pairing in [F2] then makes their classes equal. For any nonzero $q=\phi dz^2\in Q(X)$, the phase field $\mu_q=\overline\phi/|\phi|$ where $\phi\ne0$, and zero where it vanishes, is a global bounded Beltrami tensor. Indeed, its coordinate change is exactly the modulus-one rule of step 1.1: $\overline{\phi(\psi)(\psi')^2}/|\phi(\psi)(\psi')^2|=(\overline\phi/|\phi|)\circ\psi\cdot\overline{\psi'}/\psi'$. The field is measurable with norm at most one and $\langle\mu_q,q\rangle=\|q\|_1>0$. The evaluation map $A:B^\infty(X)\to Q(X)^*$ therefore is onto. Assume AC. Supply a discrete torsion-free cofinite group $\Gamma\le\mathrm{PSU}(1,1)$ acting on the unit disk $D$, the holomorphic quotient cover $\pi:D\to X=D/\Gamma$, and a finite-type compactification $\overline X$ with labeled punctures. Supply the correspondence of its punctures with all conjugacy classes of maximal parabolic subgroups of $\Gamma$, including a primitive peripheral generator at each label. Let $Y=\overline Y\setminus P_Y$ be another compact Riemann surface with finitely many labeled points removed, and let $m:X\to Y$ be an orientation-preserving quasiconformal homeomorphism extending to those labeled compactifications.

There is an orientation-preserving quasiconformal sphere homeomorphism $F$ preserving $D$, and a discrete faithful representation $\rho:\Gamma\to\mathrm{PSU}(1,1)$ with $\rho(\gamma)=F\gamma F^{-1}$. The quotient $D/\rho(\Gamma)$ is biholomorphic to $Y$ by a biholomorphism $I$ satisfying $I\overline F=m$ on the quotients. Its disk metric $2|dz|/(1-|z|^2)$ descends to a complete curvature-minus-one metric of finite area. Its puncture ends are exactly the labeled standard parabolic cusps. More precisely each has a tail isometric to $\{\operatorname{Im}z\ge R\}/\langle z\mapsto z+1\rangle$, with area $1/R$, and its holomorphic puncture coordinate is $q=e^{2\pi iz}$. Deep enough tails at all labels are disjoint and have compact complement. The primitive peripheral marking is preserved, not replaced by a proper power.

The statement includes compact $X,Y$ (no punctures), when it asserts a compact cofinite disk quotient and there are no cusp tails. It constructs a new Fuchsian model for every supplied marked quasiconformal target; no closed-only uniformization interface is used to generate punctured models.

full_proof_step_bindings.exact_quote: Pull the coefficient of $m$ back under $\pi$ to a $\Gamma$-invariant coefficient $\mu$ on $D$, with norm $k<1$. Let $r(z)=1/\overline z$. Extend it to the sphere by $\widehat\mu(z)=\overline{\mu(1/\overline z)}z^2/\overline z^2$ on the exterior disk, and give the unit circle the immaterial value zero. This formula is the coefficient of reflection-conjugation $rfr$ when $f$ has coefficient $\mu$ on $D$: direct Wirtinger differentiation gives precisely the displayed factor. Every disk Möbius transformation commutes with $r$, as follows by substituting its formula $(az+b)/(\overline bz+\overline a)$, $|a|^2-|b|^2=1$. Hence the extended coefficient is invariant under $\Gamma$. By [F1] choose its solution $F$ fixing $0,1,\infty$. Reflection-conjugation has the same coefficient and the same three normalizations, since $r$ exchanges $0$ and infinity and fixes $1$. Uniqueness gives $rFr=F$. Thus $F$ preserves the unit circle and, since $F(0)=0$, preserves its disk component. By [F2], $\rho=F\Gamma F^{-1}$ is discrete faithful; its maps preserve $D$, so lie in $\mathrm{PSU}(1,1)$. Orders and fixed-point sets are preserved, including the parabolic one-fixed-point characterization. [A1, F1, F2, F3, given, construct, algebra]

The free properly discontinuous disk action descends to an unbranched quotient cover with holomorphic sheet charts. The map $F$ descends to a marked quotient homeomorphism $\overline F$. Locally the maps $m\pi$ and $F$ have the same coefficient; [F3] makes $m\pi F^{-1}$ holomorphic with holomorphic inverse in quotient sheets. They patch to the claimed biholomorphism $I$ and give $I\overline F=m$. In particular this quotient has the supplied finite-type compactification and labeled ends, and all its maximal parabolic classes and primitive generators correspond exactly to the given ones. A maximal stabilizer is preserved under the group isomorphism and a primitive generator cannot become a proper power under an isomorphism. [F2, F3, step 1.1, given, construct, algebra]

The disk metric is invariant under its Möbius automorphisms by [F4] applied in both directions, so it descends to the quotient. It is complete: radial integration gives $d_D(0,z)=\log((1+|z|)/(1-|z|))$, and every competing curve has at least its radial integral, so bounded disk balls are relatively compact and disk Cauchy sequences converge. For quotient completeness choose a subsequence of a quotient Cauchy sequence with consecutive distances less than $2^{-j}$. Join consecutive points by piecewise smooth paths of length less than $2^{1-j}$, and lift successive paths to $D$. Their endpoints are a Cauchy sequence in the complete disk, hence converge, and projecting proves convergence of the subsequence and then of the original Cauchy sequence. For curvature, the Cayley-conjugate metric is $y^{-2}(dx^2+dy^2)$. Formula [F5] gives $\Gamma^x_{xy}=\Gamma^x_{yx}=-1/y$, $\Gamma^y_{xx}=1/y$, $\Gamma^y_{yy}=-1/y$ and all other symbols zero. For the orthonormal frame $e_1=y\partial_x,e_2=y\partial_y$, this gives $
abla_{e_1}e_1=e_2$, $
abla_{e_1}e_2=-e_1$, $
abla_{e_2}e_1=
abla_{e_2}e_2=0$ and $[e_1,e_2]=-e_1$. Consequently $R(e_1,e_2)e_2=-e_1$ and $K=-1$. [F4, F5, step 2.1, given, construct, algebra]

We prove the precise cusp embedding needed here. Work in the upper half-plane and normalize a parabolic primitive generator to a real translation of absolute length one. Its stabilizer consists of translations: an affine real map with multiplier $a>0$, $a\ne1$, conjugates this translation by suitable positive or negative powers to nonidentity translations tending to the identity. Discreteness excludes it. The stabilizer's translation lengths are a discrete subgroup of $\mathbb R$, hence cyclic: select a smallest positive length among the finitely many below any positive candidate, and use division with remainder. Use its primitive generator to normalize the length to one. For any other group matrix $g=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ with $c\ne0$, one has $|c|\ge1$. Otherwise define $g_{n+1}=g_nTg_n^{-1}$ with $T=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)$. Then $c_{n+1}=-c_n^2$ and $a_{n+1}=1-a_nc_n$. If $|c_0|=s<1$, $|c_n|=s^{2^n}$ and $|a_n|\le\max(|a_0|,(1-s)^{-1})$. The displayed multiplication also gives $b_{n+1}=a_n^2$, $d_{n+1}=1+a_nc_n$, so these distinct matrices tend to $T$, contradicting discreteness. Finally $\operatorname{Im}(gz)=\operatorname{Im}z/|cz+d|^2\le1/(c^2\operatorname{Im}z)$. For $R>1$ a matrix outside the stabilizer therefore sends $\{y\ge R\}$ into $\{y\le1/R\}$, disjoint from it. This proves precise invariance of the closed horodisk, with strict boundary slack, and injectivity of its cylindrical quotient in the surface. [step 1.1, step 2.1, given, construct, algebra]

Its area is finite, without yet assuming any cusp classification. On a punctured coordinate disk $U=\{0<|q|<a\}$ in $Y$, the map $q=a e^{2\pi iz}$ from $H^+$ is a holomorphic universal cover. The inclusion $U\to Y$ composed with this cover lifts holomorphically to $D$ by [F4]. Schwarz–Pick, after the Cayley change of variable, bounds the pulled-back quotient metric by $|dz|/\operatorname{Im}z$. Thus on $U$ its density is at most $1/(|q|\log(a/|q|))$. The area of $0<|q|<b<a$ is consequently at most $2\pi/\log(a/b)$, by polar integration. There are finitely many punctures; the remainder is compact and its smooth metric has finite area. If there are no punctures the entire surface is compact and the same conclusion is immediate. This proves cofiniteness. [F4, step 2.1, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

That closed cusp embedding is proper. Its horizontal coordinate modulo one is compact. An escaping sequence therefore has heights tending to infinity along a subsequence. The horizontal path joining a height-$y$ point to its translate by one has hyperbolic length $1/y$, so the image injectivity radius is at most $1/(2y)$ and tends to zero. Every compact subset of the surface has a positive lower injectivity-radius bound, by finite covering with small evenly covered metric balls. Thus an escaping sequence cannot have image in a compact set, which proves properness. The metric and area on its quotient are exactly $y^{-2}(dx^2+dy^2)$ and $\int_0^1\int_R^\infty y^{-2}dydx=1/R$. The coordinate $q=e^{2\pi iz}$ identifies it holomorphically with a punctured disk. Its boundary is a compact embedded circle and its interior is a component of the complement of that circle: properness makes it closed there as well as open. [step 3.1, step 3.2, construct, algebra]

Each such proper cylindrical tail eventually lies in one puncture neighborhood of the finite-type surface. Indeed after removing any sufficiently large compact core, its connected sufficiently deep tail avoids that core by properness and lies in one of the finitely many components. It cannot switch components farther down. Its primitive fundamental group specifies exactly the corresponding puncture label by step 2.1 and the supplied complete peripheral correspondence. Once its compact boundary lies outside a smaller connected puncture neighborhood which its tail meets, that smaller neighborhood lies entirely in the cusp image: the image is both open and closed away from its boundary. Thus it contains a whole tail of that labeled end. Distinct labels have disjoint deep neighborhoods; shrink the finitely many cusp tails into these neighborhoods. Their complement is compact because they cover a tail at every puncture. Positive peripheral orientation is preserved by the orientation-preserving marked homeomorphism $m$ and the holomorphic identification $I$; the generator is primitive by step 2.1. This proves every stated cusp and marking conclusion, including the empty collection in the compact case. [step 2.1, step 4.1, step 4.2, given, construct] ∎

items.actual_reading_scope_quote:
Actual reading and logical scope

The actual measurable sphere mapping, invariant-coefficient deformation, quasiconformal composition and conformality, Schwarz–Pick and covering-lift supplier proofs were read. The Shimizu iteration and proper cusp argument are given locally in the actual two-dimensional setting; a rank-two cusp theorem is not invoked for rank-one surface cusps. The construction starts with the supplied reference disk quotient and constructs cofinite models for all of its marked quasiconformal targets. It does not assume that closed-surface model theorems already include punctured surfaces, and it supplies no three-dimensional geometric finiteness or hyperbolization assertion.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Supply a torsion-free cofinite Fuchsian group $\Gamma\le\operatorname{Aut}(D)$, where $D=\{|z|<1\}$ and $D^*=\widehat{\mathbb C}\setminus\overline D$. Supply the quotient holomorphic covers and labeled standard cusp compactifications of $X=D/\Gamma$ and $X^-=D^*/\Gamma$. They have genus $g$, $n$ punctures and $2g-2+n>0$; the lower-side marking has the opposite orientation, as in simultaneous uniformization. In each puncture coordinate $\zeta$, the reference hyperbolic length element is $|d\zeta|/(|\zeta|\log(1/|\zeta|))$ after rescaling the coordinate disc.

Let $B_\Gamma$ be the complex Banach space of essentially bounded $\Gamma$-invariant Beltrami coefficients on $D$, extended by zero to $D^*$. Put $U=\{\mu\in B_\Gamma:\|\mu\|_\infty<1\}$. Let $f^\mu$ be the principal sphere solution, normalized by $f^\mu(z)=z+O(1/z)$ at infinity, and $\rho_\mu(\gamma)=f^\mu\gamma(f^\mu)^{-1}$. Write
$$Y_\mu=f^\mu(D)/\rho_\mu(\Gamma),\qquad m_\mu:X\longrightarrow Y_\mu$$
for the marked quotient induced by $f^\mu$. These quotients have labeled puncture compactifications, and $m_\mu$ extends quasiconformally across the marked points.

Use the following actual marked equivalence: $\mu\sim\nu$ if there is a puncture-preserving biholomorphism $a:Y_\mu\to Y_\nu$ such that $a m_\mu$ and $m_\nu$ are homotopic through maps $X\to Y_\nu$ extending continuously throughout the homotopy to the compactifications with all puncture labels fixed. Let $\mathcal M(X)$ be this quotient, with the quotient topology from $U$. It also represents all supplied finite-type Riemann surfaces quasiconformally marked by $X$, modulo this same equivalence.

Let $Q(X^-)$ be the finite-dimensional space of holomorphic quadratic differentials on $X^-$ with at most simple poles at its labeled punctures. For its lift $q=\phi(z)dz^2$ to $D^*$ use the norm
$$\|q\|_B=\sup_{z\in D^*}(|z|^2-1)^2|\phi(z)|.$$
The value at infinity is interpreted in its holomorphic quadratic coordinate. For every $\mu\in U$, the Schwarzian map
$$\beta(\mu)=S(f^\mu|_{D^*})$$
belongs to $Q(X^-)$, is holomorphic as a map from the coefficient Banach ball into this finite-dimensional complex vector space, and satisfies $\|\beta(\mu)\|_B\le6$. Its fibers are exactly the actual marked equivalence classes: $\beta(\mu)=\beta(\nu)$ if and only if $\mu\sim\nu$, for all $\mu,\nu\in U$.

There are an open neighborhood $W$ of $0$ in $Q(X^-)$ and a holomorphic map $\sigma:W\to U$ with $\sigma(0)=0$ and $\beta\sigma=\mathrm{id}_W$. More explicitly, the bounded complex-linear map
$$L(q)(w)=-\frac12(1-|w|^2)^2\frac{\phi(1/\overline w)}{\overline w^4},\qquad w\in D,$$
with its removable value at $w=0$, takes values in $B_\Gamma$, satisfies $\|L(q)\|_\infty\le\|q\|_B/2$, and obeys $D\beta_0L=\mathrm{id}$. The section can be chosen in the finite-dimensional subspace $L(Q(X^-))$.

The descended map $\overline\beta$ therefore gives a homeomorphism from the open quotient neighborhood $\overline\beta^{-1}(W)\subseteq\mathcal M(X)$ onto $W$, with inverse $q\mapsto[\sigma(q)]$. This is a local complex coordinate of dimension $3g-3+n$, constructed without assuming a Teichmüller manifold or using a Teichmüller metric. Chart transitions at other reference structures, a global manifold structure, completeness and skinning-map conclusions remain separate statements.

full_proof_step_bindings.exact_quote: Each invariance condition defining $B_\Gamma$ is the kernel of a bounded complex-linear difference operator on $L^\infty(D)$: holomorphic precomposition has the modulus-one coefficient factor and preserves null sets. Their intersection is closed, so it is a complex Banach subspace. Extending by zero across the circle gives an invariant sphere coefficient. By [F1], every $f^\mu$ exists, is quasiconformal, is biholomorphic on $D^*$ and conjugates $\Gamma$ to a discrete faithful Möbius group. It maps the circle to a Jordan curve and the two discs onto its complementary domains. The action on $f^\mu(D)$ is conjugate to the free proper deck action on $D$, so the quotient $Y_\mu$ is a Riemann surface with Möbius covering charts. The induced $m_\mu$ is a quasiconformal marked homeomorphism. [A1, F1, F2, given, construct, algebra]

We record the elementary Schwarzian calculations used below. For a locally injective holomorphic map set $S h=h'''/h'-(3/2)(h''/h')^2$. Direct differentiation gives $S(h\circ k)=(S h\circ k)(k')^2+S k$, and a fractional linear map has Schwarzian zero. Conversely, if $S H=0$ on a connected domain, put $p=H''/H'$. Then $p'=p^2/2$. Near a point either $p=0$ identically, or $p=-2/(z-c)$: on its nonzero set $(1/p)'=-1/2$, and the zero initial value has only the zero solution, as follows by the first nonzero Taylor coefficient if it were not identically zero. Integrating gives an affine or fractional linear map locally. Overlaps agree on open sets, hence one global Möbius map agrees with $H$ by [F5]. Consequently equal Schwarzians of two conformal bijections on the same domain make them differ by Möbius postcomposition. These statements are compatible with the infinity chart and hence also hold for the meromorphic sphere-valued bijections used here. [F5, construct, algebra]

We prepare the boundary fact needed to identify marked fibers. Hyperbolic fixed points of $\Gamma$ are dense in its circle. First a hyperbolic element exists: otherwise two nonidentity parabolics with distinct fixed points exist because the limit set is the full circle by [F4]. Normalize one as $z\mapsto z+\alpha$ and the other as a parabolic fixing $0$, in an upper-half-plane coordinate. Their product with the first raised to power $k$ has trace $2+k\alpha c$ for a nonzero real $c$; its trace has absolute value greater than two for some $k$, giving a hyperbolic element. Fix one such element with its two distinct endpoints. For any open boundary interval choose an attracting sequence with attracting point in it and one exceptional point by [F4]. At least one of the two endpoints is not exceptional, so the corresponding conjugated hyperbolic element has a fixed point in that interval for sufficiently late terms. This proves density. If a disc homeomorphism $h$ extends to the circle and commutes with $\Gamma$, it fixes every attracting and repelling hyperbolic fixed point: evaluate $h\gamma^k=\gamma^kh$ on an interior point and pass to positive or negative infinite powers. Density and continuity therefore force its boundary map to be the identity. [F4, construct, algebra]

We also prove the required round-circle gluing fact. If a $K$-quasiconformal homeomorphism $h:D\to D$ extends continuously as the identity on the circle, then its extension $H=h$ on $D$ and $H=\mathrm{id}$ on the exterior is a quasiconformal sphere homeomorphism. It is a homeomorphism by pasting the two closed topological discs. The area formula and distortion in [F2], exhausted over smaller discs, give $\int_D|Dh|_{HS}^2\le2K\pi$, since $h(D)=D$. On almost every horizontal chord, $h$ is locally absolutely continuous, and its coordinate derivative is integrable on the entire chord by this energy bound and Fubini. Its continuous endpoint values then make the fundamental-theorem formula hold on the closed chord. The function $h-\mathrm{id}$ has zero endpoints there, so extending it by zero gives an absolutely continuous function on the full line. The same argument holds on almost every vertical line. Integrating by parts on those lines and applying Fubini gives a global weak derivative equal to the piecewise derivative, which belongs locally to $L^2$. Thus $H\in W^{1,2}_{\mathrm{loc}}$, and its analytic quasiconformal inequality holds almost everywhere, since the circle has zero area and on the exterior its derivative is the identity. This is exactly [F2]'s analytic definition and proves the gluing fact without an abstract trace or removability theorem. [F2, construct, algebra]

These surfaces have genuine conformal puncture compactifications, without a hidden global uniformization assertion. Descend $\mu$ to a bounded coefficient on $X$. In a marked coordinate disc about $p$, extend that coefficient arbitrarily at the single point and multiply by a cutoff equal to one on a smaller disc. The plane coefficient extended by zero has a principal solution $u_p$ by [F1]. On the smaller punctured disc, $m_\mu$ and $u_p$ have the same coefficient in local charts. Thus $m_\mu u_p^{-1}$ is a biholomorphism from a punctured coordinate neighborhood onto the corresponding end of $Y_\mu$, by [F2]. Adjoin its missing center with this conformal chart. It has the topology of the compactification transported by $m_\mu$, and transition maps with the existing atlas are holomorphic. There are finitely many punctures and the remaining part is compact, so this produces the asserted compact Riemann surface. In these charts $m_\mu$ is $u_p$ and therefore extends quasiconformally, fixing the designated labels. Conversely, for any supplied finite-type target $Y$ and quasiconformal label-preserving marking $m:X\to Y$, lift its coefficient to $D$ and extend by zero outside. Equal-coefficient cancellation gives a marked biholomorphism $Y_\mu\to Y$ exactly as in [F4]. Hence all the supplied marked targets, rather than a restricted collection of coefficient models, are represented. [F1, F2, F4, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

The area theorem gives the needed uniform Schwarzian estimate. Normalize a univalent holomorphic disc function as $h(z)=z+a_2z^2+a_3z^3+\cdots$. The function $1/h(z)+a_2=z^{-1}+(a_2^2-a_3)z+\cdots$ is univalent on the punctured disc and fits [F3], so $|a_3-a_2^2|\le1$. Thus $|S h(0)|\le6$. Precomposing by a disc automorphism taking $0$ to $z$ and postcomposing by an affine normalization, step 1.2 gives $|S h(z)|(1-|z|^2)^2\le6$. For a sphere-valued univalent disc map, first postcompose by a Möbius map with pole outside its proper image, making it finite holomorphic; its Schwarzian is unchanged. Apply this to $f^\mu(1/z)$ and use the Möbius inversion chain rule. We obtain $|S f^\mu(z)|(|z|^2-1)^2\le6$ throughout $D^*$. [F3, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]

The homotopy constructed in step 2.3 extends continuously fixing every marked puncture. The descended $h$ is a homeomorphism of the finite-type punctured surface inducing the identity on the deck group. A homeomorphism permutes its finitely many ends, and the end classes are the distinct supplied conjugacy classes of maximal peripheral subgroups. Thus each puncture end is fixed, and $h$ extends fixing the labeled puncture points. More explicitly, normalize one lifted cusp as the horodisk $\operatorname{Im}z>T$ with stabilizer $z\mapsto z+1$. For any target horodisk level $T$, proper end preservation puts a sufficiently deep source horodisk into the preimage of that cusp neighborhood. Its image is connected and hence lies in one component of that preimage. Equivariance under the cusp generator makes this component invariant under that parabolic element, so it must be the horodisk with its unique fixed point infinity, rather than a translate based at another point. In the finite-dimensional space $Q(X^-)$ choose $d$ finite exterior points whose scalar evaluations form an isomorphism to $\mathbb C^d$. Such points exist by induction: if the previous evaluations have a nonzero common kernel, choose a nonzero element of that kernel and a point where it does not vanish, lowering the kernel dimension. A nonzero lifted holomorphic function cannot vanish at all exterior points. By [F1], each of the finitely many Schwarzian evaluations is holomorphic on the entire Banach coefficient ball. The inverse fixed evaluation matrix then makes $\beta$ holomorphic into $Q(X^-)$. Its $B$ norm is uniformly bounded by step 3.1. If $d=0$ this assertion means the constant zero map. Reflection $r(w)=1/\overline w$ commutes with every disc-preserving Möbius map. The quadratic invariance of $q$ therefore gives $F(\gamma w)\overline{\gamma'(w)}^2=F(w)$. This can also be checked by differentiating $r\gamma=\gamma r$ in the antiholomorphic variable. The hyperbolic metric identity is $1-|\gamma w|^2=(1-|w|^2)|\gamma'(w)|$. Combining the two identities proves $L(q)(\gamma w)\overline{\gamma'(w)}/\gamma'(w)=L(q)(w)$. Also $(1-|w|^2)^2|F(w)|\le\|q\|_B$ by setting $z=r(w)$. u)= eta(\mu)$. This proves the entire marked-equivalence direction without invoking a global Bers injectivity theorem. [F2, step 1.2, step 1.4, step 3.2, algebra]

Expand only the kernel: $(z-w)^{-4}=\sum_{j\ge0}\binom{j+3}{3}w^jz^{-j-4}$. This converges uniformly and absolutely for $|w|\le1$ at the fixed exterior $z$. Its terms can be integrated against the bounded function $(1-|w|^2)^2F(w)$ by uniform convergence. For each $j$, angular integration of the antiholomorphic Taylor series at radius $r<1$ gives $\int_0^{2\pi}F(re^{it})e^{ijt}dt=2\pi a_jr^j$. Fubini is legitimate since the weighted function is bounded. Consequently $\int_D(1-|w|^2)^2F(w)w^j dA=2\pi a_j/((j+1)(j+2)(j+3))$, using $\int_0^1(1-r^2)^2r^{2j+1}dr=1/((j+1)(j+2)(j+3))$. Multiplication by $(3/\pi)\binom{j+3}{3}$ leaves exactly $a_j$. The resulting series is $\phi(z)$, so $D\beta_0L(q)=q$ identically. There is no interchange of an uncontrolled double Taylor series at the boundary. [F1, step 4.1, step 4.2, algebra]

If $d>0$, apply [F5] to the finite-dimensional holomorphic equation $\beta(L(t))-q=0$ near $(t,q)=(0,0)$, whose $t$ derivative is the identity by step 5.1. It gives a holomorphic $t=t(q)$ on an open neighborhood $W$ of zero, with $t(0)=0$. Set $\sigma(q)=L(t(q))$. Shrinking $W$ makes $\|\sigma(q)\|_\infty<1$ and gives the required holomorphic section with $\sigma(0)=0$. In particular $\|\sigma(q)\|_\infty\to0$ as $q\to0$. If $d=0$, take $W=\{0\}$ and $\sigma(0)=0$. This constructs the section on the full finite-type quadratic space rather than on an assumed deformation-manifold chart. [F5, step 4.1, step 4.2, step 5.1, construct, algebra]

We have proved that $\beta$ is constant exactly on the actual marked fibers. It therefore induces an injective map $\overline\beta:\mathcal M(X)\to Q(X^-)$, continuous for the specified quotient topology because $\beta$ is continuous. Its range contains $W$ from step 6.1. The preimage $\overline\beta^{-1}(W)$ is an open quotient neighborhood of the reference class. Its map to $W$ is a continuous bijection with inverse $q\mapsto[\sigma(q)]$, continuous as the composition of the holomorphic section and the quotient map. This proves the asserted local homeomorphism and complex coordinate. The construction uses neither a metric on marked structures nor a pre-existing topology from a representation variety. Dimension is $d=3g-3+n$ by [F5], including the zero-dimensional stable case. All coefficients in the full ball were used in the fiber statement; only the existence of the section and the resulting chart were local near zero. [F5, step 4.1, step 6.1, step 4.3, step 3.3, algebra] ∎
