items.full_statement_quote:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Supply a stable finite-type reference Riemann surface $X=\overline X\setminus P$, of genus $g$ with $n$ labeled punctures and $2g-2+n>0$, together with a torsion-free cofinite disk Fuchsian model, its holomorphic quotient cover, and standard labeled cusp compactifications on both sides. Supply the complete correspondence between punctures and maximal parabolic conjugacy classes with primitive peripheral generators. The case $n=0$ is included.

A marked surface is a pair $(Y,m)$, where $Y=\overline Y\setminus P_Y$ is a compact Riemann surface with the same labeled points removed, and $m:\overline X\to\overline Y$ is an orientation-preserving quasiconformal homeomorphism preserving those labels. Two pairs are equivalent if a label-preserving biholomorphism $a:Y\to Z$ has $a m$ homotopic to the other marking through maps of punctured surfaces extending jointly continuously to the compactifications with all puncture labels fixed. Write $\mathcal T(X)$ for these classes. For $x=[Y,m]$ and $y=[Z,n]$, define
$$d_T(x,y)=\frac12\inf_h\log K_h,$$
where $h:Y\to Z$ ranges over orientation-preserving quasiconformal homeomorphisms extending to the labeled compactifications and satisfying $h m\simeq n$ in this puncture-relative sense. Here $K_h=(1+\|\mu_h\|_\infty)/(1-\|\mu_h\|_\infty)$ is the least quasiconformal constant. This also gives the usual full infimum if one initially asks only for a puncture-preserving quasiconformal map of the punctured surfaces: each such map extends quasiconformally across the punctures.

Then $d_T$ is a finite complete metric. Identify $\mathcal T(X)$ with the actual marked coefficient quotient of the local Bers theorem at the supplied reference model, and equip it with that quotient topology. The metric topology equals this topology. Every marked surface in $\mathcal T(X)$ has a cofinite disk model with the full labeled standard cusp data. Repeating the local Bers construction at any such marked base gives a chart on an open neighborhood of that point, and all these charts have holomorphic transitions. They therefore make $\mathcal T(X)$ a Hausdorff complex manifold of dimension $3g-3+n$. This includes the zero-dimensional stable case.

The coefficient change between two fixed reference surfaces is explicit. If $k:Y_a\to Y_b$ is their fixed quasiconformal change of marking with coefficient $\mu_0$, then the coefficient $R_k(\mu)$ on $Y_b$ is given in conformal coordinates, almost everywhere, by
$$R_k(\mu)(k(z))=\frac{k_z(z)}{\overline{k_z(z)}}\frac{\mu(z)-\mu_0(z)}{1-\overline{\mu_0(z)}\mu(z)}.$$
This is a biholomorphic map between the full open unit balls of bounded Beltrami sections. It induces the change of actual marked quotients. At $\mu_0$ its derivative is
$$D R_k(\mu_0)[\eta](k(z))=\frac{k_z(z)}{\overline{k_z(z)}}\frac{\eta(z)}{1-|\mu_0(z)|^2}.$$
For local sections $\sigma_a$ of the Bers maps $\beta_a$, the chart transition is $\beta_b\circ R_k\circ\sigma_a$ wherever the two charts overlap. Consequently the corresponding coefficient differential kernels are carried to one another by $D R_k$ and the chain rule. No assertion about extremal maps or a tangent norm is needed here.

full_proof_step_bindings.exact_quote: First, isolated marked points do not restrict the infimum. A puncture-preserving homeomorphism of the punctured compact surfaces extends homeomorphically over their finitely many ends: the inverse image of a compact core is compact, so each sufficiently small connected end neighborhood maps into a single prescribed end neighborhood, and the same holds for its inverse. If it is quasiconformal, extend its local bounded coefficient across the one missing point arbitrarily, cut it off outside a coordinate disc, and solve it there using [F3]. Composition with this local solution's inverse cancels its coefficient away from the center. The resulting punctured-disc biholomorphism has a continuous finite limit at the center in the target puncture coordinate. It extends holomorphically: its negative Laurent coefficients are bounded by $M r^j$ and vanish as $r\to0$. Apply the same argument to its inverse. Both extensions compose to identity on a punctured neighborhood and hence at the center by continuity. Thus it is a local biholomorphism across the center. Composing back with the quasiconformal local solution gives the claimed quasiconformal extension. This reasoning also shows that every label-preserving biholomorphism used in the equivalence extends biholomorphically to the compactifications. [F3, F4, given, construct, algebra]

For precision, bounded Beltrami sections on a fixed compact reference surface form a complex Banach space: in conformal charts the coordinate changes multiply the coefficient by a smooth modulus-one factor. A finite cover gives its essential norm and completeness by taking compatible chartwise $L^\infty$ limits. Explicitly, from an essential-norm Cauchy sequence take a subsequence with successive differences bounded by $2^{-j}$ outside a common null set in each of the finitely many charts; the representatives converge uniformly off those null sets to bounded compatible sections. The Cauchy property then gives essential-norm convergence of the whole sequence. Values at finitely many punctures are immaterial. Pullback under a supplied holomorphic disk cover is a complex-linear isometric identification with the invariant coefficient space: sheet charts give both directions, and a countable collection of sheet charts transports null sets. That cover is countable because the disk has a countable base and its fibers are discrete. By [F1], the coefficient quotient at $X$ is bijective with the actual classes just defined, not merely with unmarked targets. Every admissible marked biholomorphism or marked homotopy in one description is the same one in the other. This identifies the topology specified in the Statement with the local Bers quotient topology. [F1, A1, given, construct, algebra]

We supply the local-to-global integration needed for completeness. Let $\lambda$ be a bounded Beltrami section on a compact Riemann surface $\overline Y$ with $\|\lambda\|_\infty\le\kappa<1$. Choose finitely many coordinate discs $U_i$ and smaller discs $V_i$ with closures in $U_i$, covering the compact surface. In the $i$th coordinate extend the coefficient on $U_i$ by zero outside that coordinate domain; its norm is still at most $\kappa$. By [F3] integrate it on the sphere, obtaining a quasiconformal homeomorphism $u_i$. On $V_i$ use $u_i\circ z_i$ as the new coordinate, with the original underlying topology. On an overlap both coordinate maps have the same coefficient $\lambda$ in the old source coordinate. Their transition and its inverse are conformal by coefficient cancellation in [F3]. They form a Riemann surface atlas on the original compact topological surface. The identity map $F_\lambda$ from the old surface to the new one is quasiconformal with coefficient $\lambda$ and constant at most $(1+\kappa)/(1-\kappa)$, directly in these coordinate charts. The labeled points are the same underlying points. This constructs a compact marked limit surface, not just a structure on the punctured part, and requires no global surface uniformization theorem. [F3, F4, given, construct, algebra]

The equivalence on marked pairs is an equivalence relation: use identity and the constant homotopy, reverse the homotopy and postcompose by the inverse biholomorphism for symmetry, and concatenate homotopies after conformal postcomposition for transitivity. These operations retain joint continuity at every labeled point. Admissible maps exist, since $n m^{-1}:Y\to Z$ is quasiconformal by [F3] and has the exact required marking. If equivalent representatives are substituted, pre- and postcomposing $h$ with their biholomorphisms gives a bijection of the admissible map classes and preserves $K_h$ by the coefficient formula. Thus $d_T$ is well-defined and finite on classes. It is nonnegative, vanishes on the diagonal, and is symmetric by admissible inversion and $K_{h^{-1}}=K_h$. Given admissible maps for $x\to y$ and $y\to z$, their composition is admissible and its log dilatation is at most the sum. Choosing each map within any positive error of its respective infimum and letting that error tend to zero proves the triangle inequality. This establishes a finite pseudometric without assuming infima are attained. [F3, F4, step 1.1, given, construct, algebra]

We prove the coefficient rebasing formula and its full topological meaning. Fix any quasiconformal change of reference $k:Y_a\to Y_b$ with coefficient $\mu_0$ and let $f$ be a marked target map from $Y_a$ with coefficient $\mu$. By [F3], solving the composition formula for the coefficient of $f k^{-1}$ gives the displayed expression $R_k(\mu)$. The factors are defined almost everywhere because $k_z\ne0$ almost everywhere by the null-set transport in [F3]. Coordinate changes on source and target have the correct Beltrami phase, so the formula defines a section on $Y_b$. Pullback by $k$ identifies essentially bounded functions modulo null sets isometrically, by the null-set properties of $k$ and $k^{-1}$. Multiplication by its fixed phase is also an isometry. Pointwise disk automorphisms give $|R_k(\mu)|\le(\|\mu\|_\infty+\|\mu_0\|_\infty)/(1+\|\mu\|_\infty\|\mu_0\|_\infty)<1$. Thus $R_k$ maps the whole unit ball to the whole target coefficient ball. Its inverse is $R_{k^{-1}}$, since these are the coefficients of the successive reference changes; algebraically, with $\alpha=(\overline{k_z}/k_z)(\nu\circ k)$, it is $\mu=(\mu_0+\alpha)/(1+\overline{\mu_0}\alpha)$. Neumann expansion of the bounded multiplier $(1-\overline{\mu_0}\mu)^{-1}$, locally uniformly on coefficient subballs, proves complex Fréchet holomorphy. The same argument proves holomorphy of the inverse. Differentiation gives $D R_k(\mu)[\eta]\circ k=(k_z/\overline{k_z})(1-|\mu_0|^2)\eta/(1-\overline{\mu_0}\mu)^2$, and in particular the asserted formula at $\mu_0$. [F3, step 1.2, construct, algebra]

Every point $x=[Y,m]$ admits the full model needed to apply [F1] again. Apply [F2] to $m:X\to Y$. The model has all labeled parabolic cusps and compact complement, and the primitive generators and labels are unchanged. Reflection $z\mapsto1/\overline z$ gives its other disk quotient and conjugate standard cusp coordinates; the hyperbolic length element becomes $|d\zeta|/(|\zeta|\log(1/|\zeta|))$. Thus [F1] applies with $Y$ as new reference. Changing the marking of a target from $r:X\to Z$ to $r m^{-1}:Y\to Z$ gives a bijection of actual marked classes in both directions. Composition with $m$ or $m^{-1}$ transports each puncture-relative homotopy, so the bijection respects exactly our equivalence. It leaves the admissible maps between targets unchanged and is a pseudometric isometry. [F1, F2, F3, step 2.1, step 1.2, construct, algebra]

We give a useful metric estimate without assuming separation. For coefficients $\alpha,\beta$ on one reference, their target models have the admissible map $f^\beta(f^\alpha)^{-1}$. Its coefficient, pulled back by $f^\alpha$, has modulus $|\beta-\alpha|/|1-\overline\alpha\beta|$ by [F3]. Consequently, if $\|\alpha\|_\infty,\|\beta\|_\infty\le\kappa<1$ and $e=\|\beta-\alpha\|_\infty/(1-\kappa^2)<1$, then $d_T([\alpha],[\beta])\le\operatorname{arctanh} e$. At the zero coefficient the sharper estimate is $d_T([0],[\alpha])\le\operatorname{arctanh}\|\alpha\|_\infty$. Thus the coefficient projection is continuous into the pseudometric topology on every coefficient ball, and a holomorphic local section is continuous into that topology. [F3, F4, step 2.1, step 1.2, construct, algebra]

Let $(x_j)$ be a $d_T$-Cauchy sequence. Choose a subsequence $(x_{j_r})$ with $d_T(x_{j_r},x_{j_{r+1}})<2^{-r-3}$ for $r\ge1$. Choose representatives $(Y_r,m_r)$ of these classes and admissible quasiconformal maps $\phi_r:Y_r\to Y_{r+1}$ with $\tfrac12\log K_{\phi_r}<2^{-r-2}$, using the infimum and [A1]. Put $F_1=\mathrm{id}_{Y_1}$ and $F_r=\phi_{r-1}\cdots\phi_1:Y_1\to Y_r$. They extend to compact labeled surfaces. Induction using the admissible homotopies gives $F_r m_1\simeq m_r$ puncture-relatively, so they represent exactly the chosen subsequence. Let $S=\sum_{r\ge1}\log K_{\phi_r}<\infty$. Then $K_{F_r}\le e^S$, hence their Beltrami sections $\lambda_r$ on $\overline Y_1$ satisfy $\|\lambda_r\|_\infty\le\kappa=(e^S-1)/(e^S+1)<1$. These sections are compared on one fixed compact reference, so no varying-target coordinate norm has entered the estimate. [A1, F3, F4, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

Every coefficient in step 2.2 is realized by [F1] at its corresponding reference, by step 3.1. The maps $f$ and $f k^{-1}$ mark the same target after the change of reference. Hence $R_k$ takes the exact marked fibers onto the exact rebased marked fibers, in both directions. The commuting diagrams with the quotient projections therefore induce mutually inverse continuous quotient maps: their compositions with the quotient projections are continuous by step 2.2, which is precisely the quotient-topology criterion. They are homeomorphisms. Thus the coefficient quotient topology is independent of the chosen marked cofinite reference, and all local Bers charts based at arbitrary marked points are charts on this same topological space. [F1, step 3.1, step 2.2, construct, algebra]

The pseudometric separates actual marked classes. Rebase at $x=[Y,m]$ using step 3.1, so $x$ is the zero class. If $d_T(x,y)=0$, choose admissible maps $h_j:Y\to Z$ representing the fixed class $y$ with $\tfrac12\log K_{h_j}\to0$. Their coefficients $\alpha_j$ on $Y$ tend to zero in essential norm by [F4]. Every $\alpha_j$ represents $y$, by admissibility and [F1]'s actual fiber description. Hence $\beta_Y(\alpha_j)$ is one fixed vector, independent of $j$. Holomorphy and continuity at zero imply that this fixed vector is $\beta_Y(0)=0$. The full-ball fiber theorem [F1] says that $y=x$. Thus $d_T$ is a metric, using neither an extremal map nor a compactness theorem for minimizing maps. [A1, F1, F4, step 3.1, step 3.2, construct, algebra]

The coefficient sequence in step 3.3 is Cauchy in essential norm. Indeed the composition formula gives, almost everywhere on $Y_1$, $\frac{|\lambda_{r+1}-\lambda_r|}{|1-\overline{\lambda_r}\lambda_{r+1}|}=|\mu_{\phi_r}\circ F_r|\le k_r,\qquad k_r=\tanh\bigl(\tfrac12\log K_{\phi_r}\bigr)$. The denominator on the left is at most $2$, so $\|\lambda_{r+1}-\lambda_r\|_\infty\le2k_r\le\log K_{\phi_r}$. The right sides are summable. Completeness of the section space in step 1.2 gives a limit $\lambda_\infty$ with $\|\lambda_\infty\|_\infty\le\kappa<1$. At the finitely many marked points choose arbitrary values. The bound and all compatibility laws are preserved by essential-norm convergence. [F3, F4, step 1.2, step 3.3, algebra]

The metric topology equals the quotient topology. First the coefficient projections are metric-continuous by step 3.2. Therefore each metric-open set has open preimage under a quotient projection and is quotient-open. Conversely fix any point $x$ and a quotient-open neighborhood $O$. Rebase at $x$ by step 4.1. Its local Bers chart identifies a neighborhood with an open $W\subset Q(Y^-)$, taking $x$ to zero. There is an open neighborhood $V$ of zero in $W$ whose inverse image is contained in $O$. By continuity of $\beta_Y$ at zero choose $0<\epsilon<1$ so that $\|\alpha\|_\infty<\epsilon$ implies $\beta_Y(\alpha)\in V$. If $d_T(x,y)<\operatorname{arctanh}\epsilon$, the definition of the infimum gives an admissible map from the base representative of $x$ to a representative of $y$ with coefficient norm less than $\epsilon$. By the full fiber theorem it represents $y$, so $y$ belongs to the inverse chart image of $V$, hence to $O$. Thus a metric ball about each point of $O$ lies in $O$. This proves the reverse inclusion of topologies and the claimed agreement at every base point. [F1, F4, step 4.1, step 3.2, step 4.2, construct, algebra]

Apply step 1.3 on $\overline Y_1$ to obtain a compact Riemann surface $\overline Y_\infty$ and a quasiconformal marking map $F_\infty$ with coefficient $\lambda_\infty$. Remove the same labeled points and mark the result by $m_\infty=F_\infty m_1$. This is an object of $\mathcal T(X)$. The maps $G_r=F_r F_\infty^{-1}:Y_\infty\to Y_r$ are admissible because $G_r m_\infty=F_r m_1\simeq m_r$. Their coefficients, pulled back by $F_\infty$, have modulus at most $\|\lambda_r-\lambda_\infty\|_\infty/(1-\kappa^2)\to0$, by the inverse-composition formula. Therefore $d_T([Y_\infty,m_\infty],x_{j_r})\le\tfrac12\log K_{G_r}\to0$. The triangle inequality and the Cauchy property give convergence of the whole original sequence to the same point. This proves metric completeness, including all marked punctures. [F3, F4, step 1.3, step 3.3, step 4.3, construct, algebra]

Finally we prove holomorphic chart compatibility. Let $x_a=[Y_a,m_a]$ and $x_b=[Y_b,m_b]$ be fixed bases with their cofinite models and their local Bers data $(\beta_a,\sigma_a,W_a)$ and $(\beta_b,\sigma_b,W_b)$. Put $k=m_b m_a^{-1}:Y_a\to Y_b$. A point with coordinate $q\in W_a$ is represented by the marking of the target associated with $\sigma_a(q)$. Changing the reference to $Y_b$ replaces that marking by its composition with $k^{-1}$, so its coefficient is $R_k(\sigma_a(q))$. Thus on the open overlap the other coordinate is exactly $\beta_b R_k\sigma_a(q)$. Each factor is a holomorphic Banach-space map by [F1] and step 2.2, and hence the transition is holomorphic. Swapping the two bases proves its inverse holomorphic. Metric separation in step 4.2 makes the space Hausdorff; its charts cover every point by steps 3.1 and 4.1, and their topology is the metric topology by step 5.1. Their common dimension is $3g-3+n$ by [F1]. These facts give a Hausdorff locally finite-dimensional holomorphic atlas; second countability is proved next. In the zero-dimensional case all coordinate spaces and transitions are the unique zero-dimensional ones. [F1, step 3.1, step 2.2, step 4.1, step 4.2, step 5.1, construct, algebra]

We verify the global countability condition, rather than making a convention about manifolds. The coefficient ball is convex, and its projection is continuous by step 3.2 and surjective by step 1.2. Thus the metric space is path connected, using projected straight coefficient segments. It is locally compact by its charts and [F5]: the inverse image of a sufficiently small closed coordinate ball is compact and contains an open neighborhood of its center. Hence every point has a compact closed metric ball of positive radius. Let $s(x)=\sup\{r\in(0,1]:\overline B(x,r)\text{ is compact}\}$ and put $r(x)=s(x)/10$. This is positive, and $s$ is $1$-Lipschitz: if a closed ball at $x$ of radius $a$ is compact and $d(x,y)<a$, every closed ball at $y$ of radius less than $a-d(x,y)$ is a closed subset of that compact ball. Taking suprema gives $s(y)\ge s(x)-d(x,y)$ and the reverse inequality follows by symmetry. Every closed ball of radius strictly less than $s(x)$ is compact by this definition and [F5]. Start with a compact closed ball $K_0$ with nonempty interior. Given compact $K_j$, take a finite covering by balls $B(x_i,r(x_i))$ centered in $K_j$, and let $K_{j+1}$ be the union of the closed balls $\overline B(x_i,2r(x_i))$. They are compact and $K_j\subset\operatorname{int}K_{j+1}$. The union $V=\bigcup_jK_j$ is open. It is closed too: if $x\in\overline V$, choose $y\in K_j$ with $\delta=d(x,y)<r(x)/4$ and a covering center $x_i$ with $d(y,x_i)<r(x_i)$. The Lipschitz bound gives $r(x)\le r(x_i)+(r(x_i)+\delta)/10$, hence $r(x_i)>\delta$ and $d(x,x_i)<2r(x_i)$. Thus $x\in K_{j+1}\subset V$. Connectedness implies $V=\mathcal T(X)$. Each compact metric $K_j$ has a finite $1/l$-net for every positive integer $l$, by its ball-cover compactness. AC chooses these countably many finite nets, whose union is countable and dense in $V$. Balls of positive rational radius centered on this dense set form a countable base: inside any prescribed open neighborhood choose such a center sufficiently close and such a radius smaller than the distance to the neighborhood's complement. The space is therefore second countable. Together with step 6.1 this proves the complex-manifold assertion with the usual countability axiom. The same argument covers dimension zero; alternatively a connected discrete space is a single point. [A1, F5, step 1.2, step 3.2, step 5.1, step 6.1, construct, algebra]

The differential compatibility also has its exact local meaning. On the open coefficient preimage of an overlap, the fiber theorem gives $\beta_b R_k=\Psi_{ba}\beta_a$, where $\Psi_{ba}$ is the transition just proved. Differentiate this identity at any coefficient in that open set. Since $D\Psi_{ba}$ is invertible, it follows that $D R_k$ carries $\ker D\beta_a$ bijectively onto $\ker D\beta_b$ at the corresponding coefficient. The explicit derivative of step 2.2 specializes at $\mu_0$ to the formula in the Statement. All proofs used actual puncture-relative marked equivalence and full coefficient balls; metric completeness and topology were established before the holomorphic atlas was declared. No extremal representative, pre-existing Teichmüller manifold, global Bers theorem or tangent-norm formula has been assumed. [step 2.2, step 6.1, step 7.1, algebra] ∎

Assume AC. Supply a torsion-free cofinite Fuchsian group $\Gamma\subset\operatorname{Aut}(D)$, its marked quotient $X=D/\Gamma=\Sigma\setminus P$, its labeled standard cusp models, and the corresponding opposite quotient $X^-=D^*/\Gamma$. Here $\Sigma$ is compact, $P$ consists of $n$ labeled points, and $2g-2+n>0$. Use the local Bers map $\beta:U\subset B_\Gamma\to Q(X^-)$ and the marked equivalence relation of [[thm-local-bers-chart-for-marked-finite-type-beltrami-quotients]]. In particular equivalence is by a label-preserving biholomorphism and a homotopy of compactified markings relative to $P$.

Let $N_P=\bar\partial\mathcal V_P$ be the closed space of bounded coefficients obtained from continuous vector fields on $\Sigma$ vanishing on $P$ with bounded distributional $\bar\partial$. Identify $B_\Gamma$ isometrically with bounded Beltrami tensors $B^\infty(X)$ by lifting. Then
$$\ker D\beta_0=N_P.$$
Consequently the tangent space of this local marked complex chart is canonically $B^\infty(X)/N_P$, and its complex cotangent is canonically the space $Q(X)$ of integrable holomorphic quadratic differentials, with at most simple poles at $P$. Its tangent and cotangent norms are respectively
$$F_X(a)=\inf_{D\beta_0\mu=a}\|\mu\|_\infty =\sup_{\|q\|_1\le1}\left|\int_X\mu q\right|, \qquad \|q\|_1=\int_X|q|.$$
The first formula uses the exterior Bers coordinate $a\in Q(X^-)$; the intrinsic cotangent is $Q(X)$, not a tacit identification of these two quadratic spaces.

For marked structures represented in this chart, put
$$d(A,B)=\frac12\inf_h\log K(h),$$
where the infimum is over quasiconformal homeomorphisms in the prescribed compactified marking class relative to the labeled points. If a real-parameter chart path satisfies $\beta(A_t)=t a+o(|t|)$ and $A_0=X$, then
$$d(X,A_t)=|t|F_X(a)+o(|t|).$$
No existence of a minimizing quasiconformal map or of a minimizing coefficient representative is assumed or asserted. The conclusions apply to every supplied cofinite marked model, including the zero-dimensional stable case.

full_proof_step_bindings.exact_quote: Lifting a bounded Beltrami tensor gives a $\Gamma$-invariant coefficient with the same essential supremum: the covering is locally biholomorphic, so its transition factors have modulus one and local coordinate maps preserve null sets. Conversely every invariant coefficient descends on the evenly covered charts, and invariance identifies their overlaps. These two operations are inverse almost everywhere. They also identify $\int_X\mu q$ with the pairing computed on a measurable fundamental set. Such a set can be obtained by taking a countable evenly covered chart cover, partitioning the base into disjoint measurable subsets subordinate to that cover and selecting one lift of each subset; AC permits the selections. A discrete subgroup of the second-countable matrix group is countable: for each element choose an open basis neighborhood containing it and no other group element, giving an injection into a countable basis. Thus all fiber sums below are countable. [A1, F3, given, construct, algebra]

We record a local distance estimate using actual maps. On a small convex coordinate ball choose the holomorphic section in [F1]. Its derivative is bounded on a smaller ball, since it has finite-dimensional domain and image, hence $\|\sigma(q)-\sigma(r)\|_\infty\le C\|q-r\|$ there. Shrink the ball so all its coefficients have norm at most $\kappa<1$. The marked comparison of their models is induced by $f^{\sigma(r)}(f^{\sigma(q)})^{-1}$. By [F3] its coefficient has modulus $$\frac{|\sigma(r)-\sigma(q)|}{|1-\overline{\sigma(q)}\sigma(r)|}\le\frac{\|\sigma(r)-\sigma(q)\|_\infty}{1-\kappa^2}.$$ Consequently $d([q],[r])\le C'\|q-r\|$ after a further shrink, because $\operatorname{artanh}s\le2s$ for small $s$. We prove the specific periodization assertion needed for the derivative. If $k(w)dw^2$ is holomorphic and integrable on $D$, define on any evenly covered coordinate disc $V\subset X$ the sum of its inverse-branch pullbacks $$\Theta k=\sum_j k(g_j(\zeta))g_j'(\zeta)^2d\zeta^2.$$ Tonelli and change of variables give $\int_V\sum_j|k(g_j)|\,|g_j'|^2\le\int_D|k|$. Fix $z\in D^*$. The quadratic coefficient $k_z(w)=(z-w)^{-4}$ is holomorphic on $D$ and integrable, since its denominator is bounded away from zero there. This proves $\ker T=N_P$, including $d=0$, without assuming that a smooth isotopy integrates every distributional trivial coefficient. [F1, F2, step 2.1, algebra]

Since the local marked projection is exactly $\beta$ in its Bers chart, step 3.1 identifies its derivative quotient with the actual chart tangent. They are intrinsic under conformal coordinate changes: if $z=\psi(\zeta)$, then $\mu_\zeta=(\mu_z\circ\psi)\overline{\psi'}/\psi'$ and $q_\zeta=(q_z\circ\psi)(\psi')^2$, so $\mu_\zeta q_\zeta dA_\zeta=\mu_zq_zdA_z$. This establishes a cotangent identification on the input surface itself, rather than declaring that the exterior-coordinate differential has its $L^1$ norm on that input surface. Put $a=T\eta$. Assume AC and a supplied stable finite-type marked cofinite Fuchsian reference of genus $g$ with $n$ labeled punctures, $2g-2+n>0$. Let $\mathcal T$ be the marked quasiconformal surface space, with equivalence by a label-preserving biholomorphism and homotopy of compactified markings relative to the labeled points, and with the complex atlas and complete metric
$$d(A,B)=\tfrac12\inf_h\log K(h)$$
constructed in [[thm-marked-quasiconformal-distance-is-complete-and-bers-charts-are-holomorphic]]. Give its tangent space at each marked surface $Y$ the quotient norm $F_Y$ of [[thm-bers-tangent-quotients-have-integrable-quadratic-cotangent-norm]]. Its dual norm is the actual $L^1$ norm on the integrable holomorphic quadratic differentials $Q(Y)$.

Then $F$ is a continuous complex Finsler norm on $T\mathcal T$, and
$$d(A,B)=\inf_c\int_0^1F_{c(t)}(c'(t))\,dt,$$
where the infimum is over piecewise continuously differentiable paths in the proved complex atlas with the prescribed endpoints. No existence of a shortest path or extremal quasiconformal map is required. In particular, if a continuously differentiable map $H:\mathcal T\to\mathcal T$ satisfies $F_{H(Y)}(D H_Y a)\le rF_Y(a)$ at every $Y$ for a fixed $r\ge0$, then $d(H(A),H(B))\le r d(A,B)$.

full_proof_step_bindings.exact_quote: Work in a Bers chart centered at an arbitrary marked surface $X$. On a sufficiently small coefficient neighborhood of zero, write $T_\mu=D\beta_\mu$. Banach holomorphy implies operator-norm continuity of $T_\mu$, since the derivative is the locally uniformly convergent derivative of the local power series. Thus $T_\mu L$ is invertible near zero: writing it as $I+E_\mu$ with $\|E_\mu\|<1$, its inverse is the norm-convergent series $\sum_{j\ge0}(-E_\mu)^j$. The continuous right inverse $V_\mu=L(T_\mu L)^{-1}$ is uniformly bounded on a smaller neighborhood. Shrink the section's coordinate domain so $\mu=\sigma(q)$ lies there and $\|\mu\|_\infty\le\kappa<1$. For a coefficient variation $\eta$, rebasing at its actual marked map $k$ gives [F3]'s derivative. Multiplication by its phase and composition with $k^{-1}$ preserve essential suprema by [F4], hence the rebased coefficient has norm $\|\eta\|_\mu:=\operatorname*{ess\,sup}|\eta|/(1-|\mu|^2)$. Differentiating the holomorphic chart transition, whose derivative is invertible, shows that $T_\mu\eta=0$ if and only if this rebased coefficient has zero tangent class at $Y=[\mu]$. Indeed the target chart projection has kernel given by [F2], and the two chart projections differ by that transition. Every coefficient on $Y$ occurs under this invertible rebasing derivative. Therefore, for a tangent vector whose old-coordinate component is $a$, its intrinsic norm is exactly $F_Y(a)=\inf_{T_\mu\eta=a}\|\eta\|_\mu$. This identifies both the kernel and the infimum used here; it does not assume that the target norm is preserved by the nonconformal map $k$. [F1, F2, F3, F4, given, construct, algebra]

This weighted quotient norm is continuous. For $\lambda,\mu$ in the small section neighborhood, the weights $(1-|\lambda|^2)^{-1}$ and $(1-|\mu|^2)^{-1}$ converge in essential-supremum norm when $\|\lambda-\mu\|_\infty\to0$, and lie between $1$ and $(1-\kappa^2)^{-1}$. Thus $\|\eta\|_\lambda\le(1+\delta)\|\eta\|_\mu$ for all $\eta$, where $\delta\to0$ uniformly as the two coefficients approach each other. Given $T_\mu\eta=a$, put $\eta_\lambda=\eta+V_\lambda(T_\mu-T_\lambda)\eta$. Then $T_\lambda\eta_\lambda=a$ and $\|\eta_\lambda\|_\lambda\le(1+\delta+C\|T_\mu-T_\lambda\|)\|\eta\|_\mu$ for a uniform $C$. Take the infimum over all such $\eta$, then interchange $\lambda$ and $\mu$. This gives two-sided multiplicative norm convergence on the fixed finite-dimensional coordinate tangent space. The right inverses also bound $F_Y(a)\le C'\|a\|$, while the uniformly bounded operators $T_\mu$ give $F_Y(a)\ge c'\|a\|$. Hence the norms are jointly continuous in the base coordinate and the tangent vector. Since every point has a centered chart, $F$ is continuous everywhere. Each is a complex norm by [F2], and holomorphic chart transitions identify these intrinsic tangent classes by step 1.1, proving the asserted complex Finsler structure. The zero-dimensional stable case is the zero tangent bundle and satisfies the same assertions. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

Let $c:[a,b]\to\mathcal T$ be continuously differentiable and set $f(t)=F_{c(t)}(c'(t))$, continuous by step 2.1. By [F2] at the base $c(t)$ and the triangle inequality for $d$, the continuous function $u(t)=d(c(a),c(t))$ satisfies $\limsup_{h\downarrow0}(u(t+h)-u(t))/h\le f(t)$ for $a\le t<b$. The elementary right-Dini comparison gives $u(b)-u(a)\le\int_a^b f$: to check it, subtract the integral from $u$ and then subtract $\epsilon t$. The resulting continuous function $w$ has right upper derivative at most $-\epsilon$. If $w(b)>w(a)$, put $m=(w(b)-w(a))/(b-a)>0$. The function $w(t)-mt$ has equal endpoint values and has a minimum at some $s<b$ (if $b$ is a minimizer, $a$ also is). At that minimum its right upper derivative is nonnegative, which forces the right upper derivative of $w$ to be at least $m>0$, a contradiction. Thus $w(b)\le w(a)$; let $\epsilon\downarrow0$. Applying this to each smooth segment and using the triangle inequality yields $d(c(0),c(1))\le\int_0^1F(c')$ for every allowed piecewise continuously differentiable path. No uniform pointwise little-oh estimate along the whole path has been silently assumed. [F2, F3, step 2.1, given, construct, algebra]

Conversely let $h:A\to B$ be any quasiconformal map in the prescribed marking class, with coefficient $\mu$ on $A$ and $\kappa=\|\mu\|_\infty<1$. Use a supplied cofinite model of $A$ from [F3]. The coefficients $t\mu$, $0\le t\le1$, give an analytic, hence continuously differentiable, marked path from $A$ to the coefficient model for $\mu$, which equals $B$ by [F1]'s actual fiber assertion. At time $t$ rebase to that surface. Formula [F3] makes the tangent coefficient have norm at most $\kappa/(1-t^2\kappa^2)$. The quotient norm [F2] is no larger than the norm of this representative. Therefore the path has Finsler length at most $\int_0^1\kappa/(1-t^2\kappa^2)\,dt=\operatorname{artanh}\kappa=\tfrac12\log K(h)$, with zero length when $\kappa=0$. Taking the infimum over the actual admissible maps $h$ gives an infimum of path lengths at most $d(A,B)$. Step 3.1 gives the reverse inequality. This proves the length formula without asserting attainment of either infimum. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F4, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

Finally, under the asserted differential inequality, the chain rule for each continuously differentiable path gives $\int F((Hc)')\le r\int F(c')$. By step 3.1 the distance between its image endpoints is at most the image length. Take the infimum over paths and apply step 4.1. The resulting inequality is exactly $d(H(A),H(B))\le r d(A,B)$, also when $r=0$. This proves the global metric implication needed when a separately proved gluing or skinning map has a uniform tangent contraction. [step 3.1, step 4.1, given, algebra] ∎
